speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROTOCOL OF RATIFICATIONS DEPOSITED IN WASHINGTON
speechtext:
I should like to table copies of the protocol of deposit of ratifications of the charter of the united nations which was signed by the Secretary of State of the United States of America on October 24, 1945. Hon. members might like to have the following information in regard to this protocol:
Paragraph 3 of article 110 of the charter provides that the charter shall come into force upon the deposit of ratifications by the Republic of China, France, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and the United States of America, and by a majority of the other signatory states. Paragraph 3 further provides that a protocol of the ratifications deposited shall thereupon be drawn up by the government of the United States of America and communicated to the signatory states. The necessary ratifications having been deposited in Washington by October 24, 1945, the charter came into force and the present protocol was drawn up on that date.
Canada's instrument of ratification, following approval by parliament, was signed by His Majesty in London on November 1, 1945, and was deposited with, the government of the United States of America by the Canadian Ambassador in Washington on November 9, 1945.
Paragraph 4 of article 110 of the charter provides that:	.
The states signatory to the present charter which ratify it after it has come into force will become original members of the united nations on the date of the deposit of their respective ratifications.
Canada thus became an original member of the united nations on November 9, 1945.

Mr. Chairman, before the item is carried I should like to give my impression of certain things that have Happened in the Department of Munitions and Supply, and I think it is a most opportune time to do it when we are discussing the termination of contracts. The Progressive Conservative party cannot complain of the set-up of the various branches of the department any more than they can complain of the set-up of the various branches of the Department of National Defence, army, navy and air force.
In the Department of Munitions and Supply there was a man who grew to fame. At first he was general counsel of the department; then he became the controller of controllers. His name is Harry Borden. He was associated with another fellow named McTague, so much so that they left their government jobs together and MoTague went as counsel in Borden's office. I shall be told, as I was told last April, that Borden was a public-spirited citizen, that no one was better. I shall be told that he was a great Canadian, that no one was greater. I shall be told that he was greater than the Prime Minister, the leader of the opposition, the leader of the C.C.F., the leader of the Social Credit party, the leader of the bloc populaire, or all of them put together. That is the story that was told me at the time-that he was public-spirited. He looked after his law office very well. So much so that he took advantage of his position to fatten his law office, just as much, I will say, as the fatted calf, but before the return of the prodigal son to the Tory party. His office was the fatted calf; it grew prosperous. This man had a bird's-eye view of the department, and everyone had to go to his law firm.

He can rise on a question of privilege if I use language that is not the king's English or that would not be used in good society. What I have been saying is the truth, and it is of public interest. What I have been saying I will repeat for the information of all hon. members who were not here in April and who do not know how the strings were pulled in, the Department of Munitions and Supply by those who posed as public-spirited citizens and grabbed everything they could for their own office, and-this is even more interesting- also to collect funds for the Tory party. It was so bad that in Sarnia, for instance, it was impossible for anyone to have anything to do with the department except through the firm of Borden and Company. I have the greatest respect for the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario; he is a public-spirited citizen, and I understand his feelings, but what he has said shows that he does not know how wires are pulled before an election by those who want to take advantage of their position for party business.

I read the papers during the Grey North by-election campaign and I saw that a person was boosted to the limits by the leader of the Conservative party-the former minister of national defence for the army, who was responsible for the mess in that department during four or five years. But the leader of that political party found him very good, although at the same time he complained of the mess that was 'in that department. How could he boost the one who was responsible for it? That is beyond my understanding. But there was a reason. There was a little Borden and the loudy McTague-I will call him that.
I objected to that then, and I object to it now. Why? Because of the danger in the future. The danger of the future is not inflation. The danger of the future, the menace to this country, is the possible control of our natural resources by a gang of racketeers and filibusters who would make slaves of our fellow-Canadians. That is the danger. Inflation is nothing. Money-what is that? One has it to-day; one loses it; one has more tomorrow or one has less; it is of no importance. But if our national resources are under the control of an international finance gang, our country is finished. That is why I have always denounced those who are responsible for it. I have nothing against any one man in particular; I have nothing against Borden, against Ralston, against McTague, against Angus L. I shall make a statement, if I may. The estimates of the Department of Reconstruction have been submitted to the house under three headings:	(1) departmental
administration; (2) reconstruction projects, and (3) Canadian Arsenals Limited. I should like to point out that there has been a duplication in the first item, in that departmental administration is also in the civil estimates. I mention that so that when we discuss it now it will not be necessary to discuss it again in the civil estimates.	1
It will be noted that the estimate of requirements for departmental administration for the fiscal year was $1,500,000. Of this amount, approximately $299,295 had been spent up to August 31, leaving unexpended for the balance of the fiscal year approximately $1,200,705. This vote is for the usual expenditures incidental to the administration of a government department, salaries, telephone and telegraph charges, printing and stationery costs, etc. I will have a word to say later on the administrative organization of the department as it exists at the present time
For the second item, reconstruction projects, the estimate of requirements for the fiscal
year 1945-46 was $5,000,000. There had been expended of this amount $18,286 as of August 31. However, there are a number of commitments which were made prior to August 31 for which the actual expenditure will fall in the period from September 1 to March 31. The unexpended balance of the five million dollar vote is $4,981,714.' I shall make reference to the reconstruction projects undertaken by the department or in which the department is participating, when I discuss the work of the several administrative divisions of the department.
The third item, Canadian Arsenals Limited, calls for an expenditure in the balance of the fiscal year of $2,386,703. While a final decision with respect to the nature and size of the post-war arsenal establishment has not been made, it was considered advisable at this time to set up an organization to be responsible for the equipping, operation and maintenance of such arsenal establishments as may be established. Canadian Arsenals Limited was established for this purpose under the terms of order in council P.C. 5929, dated September 14, 1945, and will act as an agent of the government. The immediate function of the company will be to take over such part of government-owned plant and equipment as may be required in the arsenal programme. This will have the two-fold effect of expediting the reconversion of manufacturing facilities to be used in the arsenal programme and of assisting in the clearance of government-owned plant and equipment from factory premises which are not included in the arsenals scheme. Colonel M. P. Jolly, who has served as president of the crowni company, Small Arms Limited, has accepted the presidency of Canadian Arsenals Limited and will be assisted by a board of directors consisting of the following:. Mr. J. G. Notman, Brigadier A. P. Theriault, Mr. E. T. Sterne and Mr. R. M. P. Hamilton.
The Department of Reconstruction consists of the following administrative divisions: industrial reconversion branch, research and development branch, public projects branch, economic research branch, resources development branch, air development branch, war surplus branch, crown assets allocation committee, eleven regional councils, office of the labour adviser, and two crown companies, War Assets Corporation and Canadian Arsenals Limited. I shall give the house a brief description of the work of each of these units.
1.	Industrial reconversion branch. I had occasion to point out in my comments on the speech from the throne that the attaining of the objective of a high level of employment and income will depend to a great extent on

Demobilization-Reconstruction
our ability to adapt to peace-time use the industrial capacity created and expanded for war production. Much of the expanded industrial capacity created' during the war years can be readily adapted to peace-time uses. The government investment in plant capacity including tooling costs, is approximately 722 million dollars. In addition, it is estimated that private industry has expended 500 million dollars in plant expansion. Of the government investment in land, plant and tooling, approximately 75 per cent represents investments in plants wholly owned by the crown. It is estimated that at least two-thirds of this capacity can be put to good use in peace time. At the present time, arrangements have been made for the continued operation of plant capacity to the approximate total value of $210,451,000 or approximately 30 per cent of the - total government investment in land, plant and tooling. This figure represents the value of land, plant and machine tools retained by the government for operation by crown companies and the value of land, plant and machine tools sold to industry for private operation. Negotiations are under way for the disposition of a large part of the remaining manufacturing capacity created by the government. In addition to land and buildings, arrangements have also been made for the disposal of many thousands of general purpose machine tools. It is expected that within the next six-month period, all government-owned machine tools, with the exception of single purpose equipment which cannot be converted to peace-time uses, will have been disposed of to private industry. I think it can be said that the department is making satisfactory progress in converting to peace-time uses all the industrial assets created by the government investment during the war period.
Certain crown-owned plants have been set aside as multiple tenancy projects. These projects were undertaken with the objective of assisting small businesses. Space is leased at commercial rates to companies which wish to expand their operations. The tenants of the multiple tenancy projects are provided with regular services such as heat, power, freight handling facilities, etc. Each project is managed by an agent selected by War Assets Corporation. At the present time, we have two multiple tenancy projects in operation-the John Inglis ordnance plant, now known as the Liberty building comprising 300,000 square feet, and a building at Verdun, formerly operated by Defence Industries Limited. The Liberty building has 12 tenants who will have an approximate employment roll of 1,680, and the Verdun building comprising 325,000 square feet, has 28 tenants who will provide employment for 2,410 persons.
The committee will appreciate the difficulty of giving an accurate estimate of the extent to which private industry has proceeded' with conversion plane. Statistics are readily available regarding the disposal of government-owned plant and equipment but complete and accurate data with respect to the conversion of privately-owned manufacturing capacity is not yet available. However, we are able to obtain some evidence of the extent ito which private industry has undertaken its reconversion programme from the applications which have been received by the depreciation committee of the department under the terms of order in council P.C. 8640. Over one thousand applications have been approved involving new capital expenditure of approximately 200 million dollars for buildings and plant equipment. I have had prepared a statistical study of the information disclosed by 1,233 of the approved applications for special depreciation as at November 1. I would ask that this be printed in Hansard for the information of the committee.

No. This is private industry.
Employment in these 791 plants amounted to 179,000 in 1939 and rose to 345,000 in 1944. These companies expect that as a result of their reconversion plans, they will provide additional employment for some 22,000 persons within one year after the new capital expenditures have been made. In addition to employment in the plants themselves, these

Demobilization-Reconstruction
reconversion plans will provide employment for many thousands in the construction and supply industries. A considerable part of the expenditure will be made in areas where the employment problem has been aggravated by large lay-offs of war workers and the need for absorbing returning service men. For example, in the Montreal area, S22,000,000 will be spent; in Toronto, $21,500,000; in Hamilton, $9,500,000; in Kitchener and Waterloo, $5,100,000; in Kingston, $4,500,000; in Vancouver, $4,100,000; in Peterborough, $2,800,000; in Brantford, $2,600,000; in Winnipeg, $904,000; in Halifax, $226,000; and in Quebec, $341,000.
An interesting feature of these applications is the number of new lines of manufacturing which will be undertaken. From the applications now approved, it would appear that at least 100 major products never before manufactured in Canada, will be manufactured in the post-war years. These include inter-city buses, prefabricated houses, glass fabrics and plastic products, a large number of household articles, ball and roller type bearings, special type yarns, synthetic resins and medicines and chemicals. It is also significant that a number of these expenditures will be made in the smaller communities.
2.	Research and development branch. The research and development branch has been set up to provide scientific and technical assistance to industry during the period of reconversion. The branch is now operating in several fields.
First, and of most immediate importance, a technical and scientific information service has been established to serve industry and especially small industry. In each province, there have been or are about to be appointed field representatives whose duty will be to keep in touch with the industries in the province, to discuss the needs of industry and to make . available the type of technical and scientific information that small industry is unable to provide for. itself. These field representatives will make use of any local research facilities that may be available and will be assisted by a central team of six experts in the library " of the national research council. While the central service has only been operating for a few months, to date over 125 reports have been forwarded to individual companies in reply to requests for information. I cannot stress too much the importance of this service to small industry, which is seeking to improve its manufacturing techniques.
A second function of the branch will be to sponsor research in important industrial fields as a means of developing new industries in Canada.
The branch has a small headquarters staff of experts who will act as coordinators of research in broad fields. For example, the coordinator of housing research has made a most thorough and comprehensive survey of the status of housing research in Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom. Similar work is being undertaken in the communication field and a programme of cooperative research in radio link communications has been arranged as between the department, the national research council and the two railway companies. This policy of coordination will be extended to other fields as the occasion arises.
Our research and development branch has also been made responsible for the selection and dispatch of scientific -and technical specialists to Germany for the purpose of studying special targets of military and industrial interest. To date, over forty investigators have been sent to Germany. These investigators were selected on the basis of their expert and specialized experiences in the field to be covered. They have joined allied teams on arrival in the United Kingdom and are now investigating special .targets in nearly every field of scientific and industrial technology. The reports prepared by these allied teams will be made available to Canadian industry. In addition to reports on specific subjects, much information of a general nature on industrial processes and techniques is also being obtained. This information will be of inestimable value to Canadian industry at this time, when old industries are being revitalized and new industries created.
3.	Economic research branch. It will be evident from a reading of the government White paper, "Employment and Income", that a successful carrying out of reconstruction policies will depend on our ability to forecast economic trends in the various parts of the country. Such forecasts can only be made if we have reliable statistics and economic data. It is the function of the economic research branch to collect these statistics and to interpret them in terms of employment and income levels. While the branch has a statistical unit of its own, full- use is being made of all research facilities now available in other government departments.
4.	Public projects branch. It is the responsibility of the public projects branch to obtain complete information upon all public projects whether they be initiated by the dominion government, the provincial governments or the municipalities, or jointly. 8.	Office of coordinator of regional reconstruction councils. The work of reconstruction is by its very nature a major undertaking which will require the concerted action of the federal government, the governments of the provinces, the municipal authorities, industry, labour, agriculture and the other economic groups in our society. Such concerted action will be possible only if each of the government authorities and each of the various economic groups assumes its appropriate responsibilities and only if there is a complete coordination of the programmes which may be initiated by the dominion government, the governments of the provinces and the municipalities. It seemed obvious that if this very desirable objective were to De attained, there should be established regional organizations which would act at once as interpreters of dominion government policy on reconstruction matters in the region concerned, and as media of first hand information for the Department of Reconstruction on reconstruction problems in that region. It was decided, therefore, to establish regional councils. There is one regional council in seven of the provinces and two of such councils in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. The chairman is an appointee of the Department. of Reconstruction and represents the dominion government on the regional council. In order to coordinate the work of the various councils, there has been established with headquarters in Ottawa, the office of the coordinator of regional councils. In defining the functions of the councils, account has also had to be taken of the veiy different problems which will arise in the various parts of the country. However, the general functions of the councils can be described as follows:
(i)	To assist the dominion Department of Reconstruction in assembling information relative to the problems of reconstruction in their respective regions and in keeping such' information up to date.
(ii)	So to organize the respective regions that-(a) information concerning local reconstruction problems and concerning reconstruction legislation and policies shall be easily accessible to all concerned;
(b) all reconstruction activities within each locality shall be known and coordinated.
(iii)	To cooperate closely with provincial departments of reconstruction and, directly or
through local committees, with all organizations havihg to do with reconstruction problems;
(iv)	To encourage provincial and municipal authorities to have ready proper plans and specifications for capital projects which it is desired to carry out as soon as conditions of employment justify, with particular reference to-
(a)	works which provincial or municipal governments wish to carry out in the normal course as soon as labour and materials are available;
(b)	useful works which might be carried out at times when it is desirable to increase employment within the areas concerned.
(v)	To advise the minister and the department from time to time on reconstruction matters relative to the separate regions.
I feel that our solution of a number of reconstruction problems can be assisted greatly if the provinces, the municipaliites, industry, labour, agriculture and the other economic groups concerned will make use of the facilities offered by the regional councils. These councils will have complete information on the policies of the dominion government, and inasmuch as they represent all sections of the community, can serve a most useful purpose. Criticism has been made during the war years of the tendency to centralize administrative functions in Ottawa. The existence of the regional councils is an attempt to meet that criticism in the period of postwar reconversion and reconstruction. As a minister of the crown, I am, of course, always pleased to meet delegations from the various parts of Canada. However, I suggest that if full use is made of the facilities available in the regional councils, much time and expense will be saved by those who wish to submit their reconversion or reconstruction problems to the dominion government.

Mr. Chairman, I for one shall be glad when we have completed the consideration of the minister's estimates, because personally I find it monotonous to be as critical as I have had to be these last three days. I hope the committee will appreciate the fact that at the present time there is unfolding in the town of Leaside a tragedy which seems about to enter its final act. It is going to require determined action on the part of parliament to prevent this tragedy from proceeding to the final curtain. I hope the committee will appreciate the immensity of the factors involved, and for that reason I am going to give. some figures which will illustrate the tremendous size of the enterprise and the extent of the threatened loss.
I have no thought of mere carping criticism. On the other hand it is our duty to be constructively critical. In this situation I hope that it is yet not too late, and that if parliament makes its voice clearly heard, the minister will stop this tragedy. I refer to Research Enterprises Limited at Leaside in the county of York. This enterprise is one of the greatest in Canada's whole record of achievement in the field of wartime production. It is one of the marvels of industrial enterprise wrought by Canadians during the war. Every Canadian has a right to be proud of it; every Canadian has an interest in it. Every Canadian has an interest in preventing its becoming the subject of a colossal national tragedy.
The corporation in question is a crown corporation. I want to refer in introducing this subject to a description of it given by

Professor E. F. Burton, who is director of the Department of Physics at Toronto university, an eminent scientist who had much to do with the original proposals for the erection of the plant and the commencement of the enterprise which later took the form of Research Enterprises Limited. According to a return tabled in the house by the minister on October 13, we find that the corporation was organized in September, 1940. The buildings erected at this very large plant number twenty. The expenditure to acquire the assets involved was as follows: Land, $134,992.72; buildings, $3,525,181.77; machinery and other equipment, $5,400,0531.70; total expenditure on plant and equipment, over $9,000,000.
With that plant and equipment a marvel of production was achieved, amounting, according to the answer given in HansUrd at page 1826 of November 5, to $230,000,000 as of November 2, 1945. Imagine, $230,000,000 of production at that plan t I That is a great achievement, in which all Canadians may well take pride. I should like to quote from an outstanding address that was given by Professor Burton at the annual meeting of the Ontario Educational Association in Toronto in April, 1944. Speaking of the company he said:
This is a crown company formed by the federal government, at the instigation of the national research council, but under the management of an independent board of directors nominated by the ministry of munitions and supply. While projected in the first instance for the manufacture of optical glass and optical instruments for the armed services, from the beginning it has produced also various secret devices connected with Radar.
The necessity of war-supply in Canada has led to extensive production in fields of manufacture entirely new to this country. This work necessitated not only the construction of extensive buildings and the purchase of large quantities of highly specialized equipment, but it has developed a comprehensive practical knowledge of production methods in fields hitherto unknown in Canada.
This company is unique among Crown companies for the fact that it did not develop from nor was it based on, any manufacturing concern, or group, already engaged in some form of munition production. In spite of the fact that it began only in September, 1940, it has grown until it now comprises some twenty buildings and over 7,000 employees. Its annual production is valued at many millions of dollars.
Roughly speaking, the operations of the company are along two main lines:	(1) optical
glass and optical instruments, and (2) special radio equipment used in Radar. The relative monetary values of the outputs of these two divisions are in the ratio: optics 3 to radio 11.
Although the word "research," appears in the title of the company it is purely a producing company. Of course, problems are continually arising which need immediate solution and, as a consequence, a considerable amount of develop-

Demobilization-Reconstruction
menit engineering has always been in progress. Many operations have been improved, and new devices designed, so that the term "research" is really not a misnomer.
I shall come back to that address later.
This enterprise has also been eminent, I should almost say unique, in respect of its industrial relations, because throughout the entire five years during which it has been in operation, industrial harmony has prevailed in the plant. The workers are organized in local 1039 of the United Steelworkers of America, C.I.O., and they have been given creditable leadership by the union officials. I pay my tribute to the responsible executive leaders * of that union for the constructive work they have done in connection with that plant.
The immensity of the undertaking may also be appreciated by the fact that there are over
1,000	classifications of employees of all kinds. This will give the committee some idea of its size and importance and some conception of the extent to which skills have been developed at this plant. Let it not be said that they were only partial skills, or that it was just a case of a worker fitting into some minute place in a long assembly line. Not so; the efforts involved in the operation of the plant are of a highly skilled nature. I go further and say that there have been developed in this plant skills and techniques which are new in Canada. I should like to refer to a return that was made to this house on October 13 by the Department of Reconstruction. I asked for certain figures in regard to the number of employees, and this was the information I was given. The number of employees at the peak of production was 7,518. Now, watch the drop that has occurred in recent months. The day before V-E day, last May, saw a drop in the number of employees to 5,552. On the day before V-J day the number had dropped to 4,896, and on October 1 it had dropped to 3,187. To-day I am informed that the number of workers at that plant is less than 2,300. So that there has been a steady decrease.
By way of illustration of the point I made in regard to the introduction of new skills, I should like to refer to another return, No. 5. I had asked how many persons were brought to Research Enterprises from outside Canada to work at the company's plant at Leaside. The answer was fifteen, of whom thirteen were .brought from the British isles and two from the United States. Those men introduced new skills. I happen to know something of the work that was done, and I say, and I think the committee should have full appre-47696-149
ciation of the fact, that new skills and new techniques hitherto not developed in Canada were developed in this great plant. If these new skills and techniques, having taken years to develop, are dissipated, it will take years to replace them.
I am not going into details of production at the plant. I have already said it was a marvel of production. I am not going into the technical aspects, because I am not a technician. But one might refer to the place that radar had in the winning of the war. It was Sir Stafford Cripps who said that if any one factor contributed more to the winning of the war than anything else, it was radar, and this is the plant in which radar was developed. The manufacture of optical glass was carried on at that plant, something that was brand new in Canada. Nowhere else in Canada has optical glass been manufactured.	.
May I refer to one or two other answers that were given at page 1811 of Hansard of November 5, in reply to questions I had asked in respect to Research Enterprises. Of the total production of $230,000,000, radar represented approximately 80 per cent, optical instruments 19^ per cent, and optical glass one per cent.
I shall not take time to dwell on the research that has been developed at the plant, because that was ably covered by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce), speaking in the house on October 30, as reported at page 1658 of Hansard. What I have said up to this moment has been descriptive of the enormous scope of the undertaking, the tremendous contribution it has made to the winning of the war, and its value as a national asset to Canada.
Now I come to another part of the story which cannot be painted in glowing colours, but only in dark tones. It is the beginning of the tragedy of disintegration. One of the things the Minister of Reconstruction has done has been to sell one of the buildings. Let us be quite clear in our understanding of this. I do not think any of us would object to the sale of any of these buildings if we could see that by that sale there was a guarantee of employment and of good wages and working conditions, and as well the assurance that no serious damage would be done to the possibilities of development or use of the rest of the plant. But what do we find? One building has been sold out of twenty. It was sold on June 15 to the Corning Glass Company. That company is, it is true, a glass manufacturing company, but it is not a manufacturer of optical glass.

Demobilization-Reconstruction

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Oh, oh.

I am speaking of their operations at the plant in question, not of their operations in the United States.
' Mr. HOWE: Let me say that the Corning Glass Company have made three-fourths of all the optical glass that has been made in the United States in the war period.
I made it quite clear that I was not speaking of the operations of Corning Glass Company in the United States; I am speaking of the operations in the building they purchased from the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: They are not operating there. The building has not been delivered to them.

Building No. 14 was sold to the Corning Glass Company for $150,000 on June 15 of this year. If you will look at the return I am referring to, questions 2 and 3, October 17, you will find that the original cost of that building was $522,000. It was sold to the Corning Glass Company on June 15 for $150,000-less than a third of the cost. What guarantees were obtained as to employment or wages or working conditions? None. The return I have referred to shows that the Department of Reconstruction obtained from the Coming Glass Company no undertaking or agreement whatever in regard to maintenance of employment, maintenance of wage rates, continued union recognition.
The glass plant at Research Enterprises where optical glass was made is building No. 2. That building to-day is being used simply for the storage of benches and desks. No production is being carried on there. The building sold was not the glass plant; it was No. 14, the mobile assembly plant.
It is apparent that the department not only is prepared to sell buildings with little regard to the maintenance of employment, but has been taking no steps to prevent destruction of equipment. May I just here refer, to the fact, which you will find on page 604 of Hansard, that when building No. 14 was sold to the Corning Glass Company no other tenders were called. There were no tenders for a building which represented one of the most important assets of that great enterprise. Now, where the plant assets of the country are sold, it surely should be on a basis of calling for tenders and fair prices, with some assurance of employment.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North referred the other evening to this matter of destruction of equipment, and to certain questions and answers to be found at page 603 of Hansard. I quite agree with the hon. member's interpretation of the third question, in which he asked, referring to this destruction

of equipment: "Did any of the employees ask permission to buy material *which is being destroyed?" The answer given was yes, and that Research Enterprises Limited had no authority to sell.
This matter of destruction of equipment belonging to the country was discussed in the House of Commons. The hon. member for Red Deer discussed in this house on September 17, and in the Toronto Globe and Mail of September 18, page 2, there appeared an article headed, "Asks Commission Probe Destruction of War Materials." It is a staff report to that newspaper, based largely on the remarks made the previous evening by the hon. member for Red Deer. That statement in the Globe and Mail was noted by the employees in the plant, and I will read now a statement signed by twenty-one persons. who were employees of the plant at that time. It bears their signatures, and is dated September 18, the day on which that article appeared in the Globe and Mail:
In reference to morning paper of September 18, 1945 re breaking up of radar equipment, 'we the undersigned state that we either assisted or watched employees of R.E.L. dismantle and break up monitor chassis No. 11 of R.X.F. unit.
There were over 250 monitor No. 11 chassis broken up on September 13th and 14th and 17th instant.
I suggest that this matter calls for an accounting on the part of the department, and the department owes the House of Commons a frank and complete answer on at least these points: (1) On whose orders was that valuable radar equipment destroyed? (2) Was it done with the knowledge of the department at the time? (3) What knowledge has the department gained of this destruction of radar equipment since? (4) What steps has the department taken in the light of the knowledge so obtained?
I said something on the subject of trying to be constructive in our approach to these problems. We are not 'underestimating the size or the gravity of the problem. Here is a great national asset with a wonderful record in time of war. What are we going to do with it? Well, there are many peace-time uses to which this plant could be put. As long ago as a year and a half Professor Burton, this great authority who had so much to do with the commencement of operations at this plant, laid before the public and the government some concrete proposals. I quote from the speech of Professor Burton to the Ontario Educational Association. He opened that part of his address with these words:
It should be pointed out particularly that the company has gathered together into one team a large number of capable scientists and technical

Demobilization-Reconstruction
men-chemists, engineers and physicists-whose services should be retained, if possible, for future operations.
Then he goes on to discuss particularly the post-war possibilities of this great plant:
The scale upon which the operations of the company are carried on is so vast, that it is out of all proportion to any, conceivable comparable operation in peace time. Still, it is one unit in wartime industry which will have to be considered whenever "full-time post-war employment" is considered. The future might well be dealt with under the following three main headings:
(1)	instrument division
(2)	radio division
(3)	glass-making division
(1)	Instrument division. The type of production during war time has been limited to articles required by the services, such as telescopes, sights, and range-finders-but this work has esatblished in Canada a completely new industry. There is ample accommodation in equipment and supply of personnel to maintain a very efficient and paying business, not only in all kinds of optical instruments, but in the manufacture of general scientific apparatus to meet the demands of schools and colleges throughout Canada.
Practically every item in the latter category was imported from foreign sources before 1939. It will be nothing short of a calamity if we let this business slip from our hands.
Inasmuch as these facilities have produced technical equipment for the services, there can hardly be any doubt that these services will wish to keep at least a skeleton organization for future development. This could well share in an arrangement under which general scientific apparatus might be produced.
(2)	Radio division. The construction involved here practically all belongs to the secret
' category and constitutes .an entirely new development in the broad field of radio. No one can guess at its future but it opens great vistas of advance for all civil transportation and navigation problems.
(3)	Glass-making division. Here, again we have an industry completely new to Canada, and here also the company has built up a very efficient organization from the point of view of both labour and technical staff. There is no doubt that the company is turning out vast quantities of optical glass which is equal in quality to any in the world. The company has benefited by the experience of some of the oldest glass firms in Great Britain and America. The particular success in this field is largely due to the lifetime experience of the president, Colonel W. E. Phillips, in the glass industry.
Aftdr going on to emphasize the calamity that would befall this country, if this plant, the scientists and technicians assembled in it were simply allowed to disintegrate, Professor Burton points out the needs of the schools and colleges and educational institutions in Canada for scientific equipment of the kind which has been produced in the plant, and which could still be produced, and has this to say concerning the danger of the plant falling into the hands of an international cartel:
47696-149J
Unless we wake up to the insidious .action of this international movement tending to handcuff production in as many countries as possible, we in Canada will revert to the position of "hewers of wood and drawers of water" for some fascist state of the future.
I appeal to you all-
This is his appeal to school-teachers in the province.
-to use your influence with the people and particularly, the public men in Canada to make every effort to retain for peaceful ends what has accomplished such a fine job for the war.
The need for action is immediate-
That was April, 1944. We are sitting here on November 21, 1945, a year and a half later.
-because, as war production falls off, the technical staff of Research Enterprises Limited, employed in the design of apparatus could be put immediately on the design of school and college apparatus. We cannot wait for the .actual end of the war in order to be ready for peace.
These. are prophetic words. Professor Burton also had this to say:
I wish to make a special appeal for your support in every public w.ay possible for the retention, for the people of Canada, of the skills and personnel which have developed in such a great way during the years of war.
Has Professor Burton changed his opinion? No. I made a point to communicate with him and got his opinion on the point, and this is what he said on November 10:
I feel just as strongly in regard to this matter as I ever did, and have no objection whatever if you quote my opinion on any occasion. At the present moment, the universities of Canada are in a quandary with regard to the purchase of scientific apparatus, and the country will probably be buying from the United States several hundred thousand dollars worth of scientific apparatus which, with some reasonable forethought, might have been produced in our own country and at Research Enterprises Limited. I thoroughly believe that if we had approached the matter of making scientific apparatus for peace in the same spirit in which we made the scientific apparatus for war, we would be in a satisfactory position at the present time and would have already established in the country a worthwhile scientific manufacturing institution.
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd.) E. F. Burton,
Director.
We have heard a good deal in the house, and properly so, and particularly from the hon. member for Nanaimo, about the imperative necessity in these days, and in the days to come, of closely coordinating our national defence plans with industry. Here is a plant that produces radar, one of the things that contributed most to the winning of the war, and apparently the government is just sitting back and watching this great undertaking disintegrate, watching the technicians and scientists leave to seek employment elsewhere. The future of this plant is definitely and intimately related to the whole programme of
Demobilization-Reconstruction

national defence in this country. On the one hand we dare not lose' control1 of Research Enterprises Limited, mor on the other hand dare we fail to carry on the work that has been done there in the development and manufacture of radar.
Is there anyone who will venture to say that we have even begun to tap the ultimate possibilities of radar? Look at this great country of ours. The uses that radar could be put to in Canada are simply infinite. The needs of radar throughout the world at the present time cannot be exaggerated. Here is this great plant. Are we to maintain the manufacture of radar at this plant? It might be likened to a permanent arsenal. I suggest that the words of the hon. member for Nanaimo, words of warning about the necessity of coordination of our industrial plants with our defence plans were timely words of warning.
I am not going to belabour the subject of research which was covered so fully by the hon. member for Parkdale in his great speech on this subject on October 30. Fortunately there is little left for me to say on that subject. The amount which is being made available by the government for expenditures on research is lamentably small. If we as a government and a parliament are to contribute what we ought to be contributing to the development of this country, to the development of its tremendous potentialities, we must give every possible encouragement to industrial research. Here is a plant which in the narrow sense of the word is not a research plant alone; it is in one aspect a pilot plant, the kind of plant necessary to carry research plans into industrial facts. It is only by a plant like this that the plans which are worked out in laboratories by laboratory technicians in research operations can be translated into fact. Dare we go on and starve this plant out? If we do, it will be nothing short of a national calamity. I think parliament ought to be fully conscious of the tragedy that is apparently moving on to its conclusion.
In my closing remarks I wish to refer to some questions of mine which are found at page 1811 of Hansard. Question No. 8 was this:
What attempt, if any, has been made to adapt (a) the products; (b) the producing capacity, of this company to peace-time uses?
The answer was:
Discussions have taken place with national research council and the Department of Transport on the adaptation of certain products to civilian and other use.

Question No. 9 was:
What attempt, if any, has been made to make the -products of the company available to educational- institutions and research laboratories?
The answer was:
Answered by 8.
Question No. 10 was:
What assets of the company have been listed with War Assets Corporation for disposal?
The answer was:
Land, buildings, equipment and materials, as they have become surplus to company needs, have been so declared to War Assets Corporation over a period of several months.
Question No. 11 was:
Are the buildings of the company available for rent or sale?
The answer is, Yes; under certain conditions.
Apparently there is no plan that the Department of Reconstruction has for the retention or use of this great undertaking. Seemingly it is simply to be put up on the auction block, piece by piece. If prompt action is not taken soon to preserve the essential parts of this plant for the need that I have mentioned, the need of defence and the development of radar, then a national tragedy will have been consummated. Where are the government's promises of full employment? What about the fulfilment of the government's promises and' extravagant talk of full-time employment? How about a little fulfilment of the promises? Are we simply to stand by and hold our hands, as the government is apparently doing, and watch the disintegration of this corporation and the disbandment of this competent, staff of scientists and technicians? Are we to watch the dissipation of skills that are new in Canada? If we are, then I say we are content to witness a national catastrophe. That may be strong language; it is not too strong in the circumstances. For years we have been talking about the necessity of our attracting whole new industries to Canada. Everybody has been saying, let us have new skills introduced in Canada; it is the best thing for the country; let us have all the new skills we can get. Here is one case where new skills actually were introduced in a marvellous way, and to-day we are simply sitting back and watching the whole thing being disbanded. With our arms folded, we are watching it disintegrate. I suggest that the time has come when we must demand action from the government.
The need for pressing on with research, the need for retaining all the scientists we have in this country was never more apparent than it is to-day. I would quote some remarks made

Demobilization-Reconstruction
by the president of Toronto university, Doctor Sidney Smith, at an industrial scientific research conference held in Toronto in June last:
I place it before you, gentleman, as a problem of major importance and of considerable size; the problem of retaining the research men in Canada. Are we going to train these men for industry and research institutions in Great Britain and the United States? I know your answer will be, "no." The universities are looking to you for assistance in promoting research to the end that the best brains in this particular activity may be kept in Canada for the development of Canadian industry and the development of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the speech made by the member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) and the speech made by the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Fleming) with reference to Research Enterprises. I think they both shbw a colossal misconception of the part that Research Enterprises plays in the industrial life of 'Canada. The hon. member who last spoke said he thought it necessary to be critical. I think he paid me and the Department of Munitions and Supply an appreciable compliment. Research Enterprises was started from the grass roots late in 1940. It was completed under the guidance of the Department of Munitions and Supply, and particularly the guidance of the national research council, and it was able to produce $268,000,000 worth of production from the date of its completion up to the present time.
My hon. friend has suggested that it is a pilot plant. I may say that I never knew a pilot plant produce on that scale. I wish to make it quite clear that this is a manufacturing plant and nothing else. It was built to produce in volume the inventions and developments of the national research council. That is the role it has had. Every article,	with very few exceptions, was
developed in the form of a prototype in the laboratories of the national research council in Canada and was sent to Toronto for manufacture. That is the function of the plant. It is a manufacturing plant. The tools needed are manufacturing tools. Research is carried on at Ottawa; development work is carried1 out at Ottawa, and the manufacturing is done in Toronto.
I made it a condition when the plant was built that it would not be a research plant. All my experience has indicated that such a plant should be one thing or the other, either a research laboratory or a manufacuring plant. The first suggestion was that this plant should be built-in Ottawa, and Dean Mackenzie agreed with me that it would be well to put it in another city so that we
would not have those concerned with research interfering with the operations of the plant, and so that it could be made clear that it was a manufacturing plant and not an experimental laboratory.
The plant has been producing at the rate of something over $8,000,000 a month for a great many months. What has it been producing? 1 turn to page 1812 of Hansard where my reply appears to questions asked by the hon. member who has just spoken. The total production of approximately $230,000,000 as of November 2, 1945, appears on that page. The question was asked, what was the production? The answer was that radar represented eighty per cent. That means that radar was $180,000,000. What are the peace-time uses of radar? There are a few limited uses and' one will come into being on ships. Almost in a day or two we have produced all the radar equipment for ships of the most modern type, and I may say that we are rather advanced in comparison with other countries in that we 'have produced all the radar equipment for which we have ships to use it, ships on the Canadian register. It is all there in the plant, and we are making arrangements to work out some practical scheme of renting the equipment to ships for use.
I wonder if anyone has any conception of what $180,000,000 worth of anything is. It is a tremendous amount. My hon. friend said that Professor Burton had stated that for the next few years we would be probably importing $500,000 worth of school equipment from the United States.
Scientific instruments.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Well, we could make $500,000 worth of scientific instruments in this plant in two days.
You would not expect anything else of a professor, would you?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: That is typical of Professor Burton, with whom I have been associated.
Some professors have done a good job in this war.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
He is a professor of physics, and when you say that you have told the whole story. To go on with the enumeration, optical instruments represent 19^ per cent, and that would represent about $45,000,000 worth of such instruments. We have in store in the plant optical glass to fill any possible requirements of Canada for two years, and we made that in one day. There is $40,000,000 worth of optical instruments, and I do not need to elaborate on the chance of that being
Demobilization-Reconstruction

disposed of or of our being able to sell $40,000,000 worth of optical instruments over the next twenty years.
Research Enterprises is a war plant. True, it employed at its peak 8,000 men. The Bren gun plant employed 14,000 at its peak and to-day it is not employing any people on the type of work it did at that time. . Research Enterprises is making radar equipment and special optical instruments which are not required in peace time. The two plants are exactly on a par as far as that is concerned.
We could hold that vast plant as a standby. We could manufacture radar for anyone who might need it. We might say, We will save the plant so 'that we can manufacture this equipment, although we have enough optical glass for two years. But at the end of two years, it may be said, we may need more and more, and we will save the plant for that purpose. We have enough optical instruments left from the pipeline to supply Canada for the next four or five years. We are sellers of optical instruments in a big way, if anyone wants telescopes or binoculars. We can sell these things on a wholesale basis and we shall have them in stock for a considerable time.
That is the situation at Research Enterprises. Now, here is a great plant the work for which has ended, and the question is, shall we keep the plant for its original purpose? Shall we keep the machinery? We cannot sell the product unless the government proposes to spend $8,000,000 a month to keep the staff employed. Otherwise, I do not know of anything that they can make in quantity which could be used. That is one question. The next is, should we use the plant to provide a centre of employment for the same skills that we used1 there, by turning it over to private enterprise which can manufacture and sell on a scale that will mean real employment.
The hon. member spoke about bringing in Corning Glass. Coming Glass has done a fine job throughout the war years. We manufactured optical glass at Research Enterprises by a process we borrowed from the United Kingdom. We borrowed it for the duration of the war, and we have a firm undertaking that we have the right to the process only for the duration of the war. In. other words, unless we can make some agreement with Chance Brothers, who own the rights, we are out of business in any event, with the present process.
Another factor has come in, and that is that glass used in optical instruments made for war purposes in the United States has been made by a different and considerably
	-
cheaper process. If in ken or fifteen years we need to come back to a large scale production of optical glass we would certainly use a process more modern than that now installed at Research.
Why did we bring in Corning Glass? May I say that I brought them in on the advice of the president of this plant. He gave me as his reason that Canada should have a glass industry, that Corning were the most modern people, and that he thought it would be a fine potential for war to have them established in Canada.
We sold a building. That was a building for a special purpose, and it was not one readily convertible to any particular manufacturing process. We built it under an agreement with Corning that they would spend $800,000 in remodeling and reequipping the building, and that they would bring to Canada a part of their production which would be new to the Canadian market.
True, we got a price for the plant which took account of the fact that extensive alterations and remodelling would be necessary. I think that is reasonable; we have done it elsewhere. We must always consider that a plant built for one purpose may not be readily convertible to another purpose.
Mr. MaeNICOL :	Nor the machines,
either.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
This was purely a matter of a building. However, we brought in Coming because we believed that we were bringing in a desirable new industry in the glass field, and that we were bringing in an industry which would use skills which were available in that area. We believed that we were safeguarding the requirements of Canada in the event of another war, so far as optical glass is concerned.
I can tell my hon. friend that for a long time we have had plans as to what we are going to do with this other building. The difficulty in announcing it is that we have not finished with this war. There are still contracts that have not been cancelled, outstanding at Research Enterprises for some $30 million for war equipment. It is necessary to finish those contracts-and this will take until April of next year-before we can consider any further disposal of the building. But when that time comes we shall have tenants there that will use skills of a tpye which were employed in Research Enterprises. The volume of employment will not be as high as it was during the peak period; but on the other hand we shall have at least
3,000	people employed in that property, when

Demobilization-R econstruction
our present plans mature. I dlo not know of any other procedure which would permit em. ployment to that extent in that area.
I believe that it is a practical approach to reconversion in this instance. I am perfectly sure that the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, who is financial critic for the official opposition, would disapprove if the government spent $8 million a month, as it has been doing for several years, to maintain employment in that plant. I am perfectly certain no one can suggest any output of radar equipment, optical instruments, or optical glass which would justify anything like the employment we visualize as a result of the conversion that is in process at that, plant.
It has been a great experience to be associated with the plant. The hon. member has spoken about the scientists there. Most of the scientists were on loan from the national research council.
One of those professors the minister was talking about a little while ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: He was borrowed. Many scientists worked between the research council and that plant. But on the strength of the plant itself there were not many men who qualified as pure scientists. Those who have so qualified will be absorbed into the national research council. We are short of scientists; we need everyone we can get. For instance, we need them for Chalk River. Steps have already been taken to retain those men who have special skills which would be valuable in the future work of the national research council.
Is provision being made for paying them decently, so that we can prevent their going to the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Steps are under way to that end. We are paying a bit more now than we did before, and we hope to do better still.
The skills will be preserved. Any equipment of special value for scientific work will be moved to Research laboratories. Skeleton equipment will be preserved at Research Enterprises. It is not intended to sell the glass section of the plant, since it is not readily convertible for any other use. We are turning that over to Canadian Arsenals Limited. In the buildings which make up the present glass plant will be a skeleton of sufficient size to carry out all the operations which were carried out in the Research Enterprises plant itself.
In this way we shall preserve all the techniques, and take care of all the special skills.
There are not so many men having great skill in the plant. Most of them were men who acquired their skills in a. short time, and who could readily convert those skills to other types of production. We are going to use the plant in the only practical way I can think of, which would bring a substantial employment into that area; and we are going to complete that reconversion as soon as we can clear the plant of its war work.

The minister has not answered clearly some of the questions which were asked. I am led to believe that Research Enterprises Limited is to be closed down for all practical purposes by next April. Am I right or wrong in that inference ?
Then, I should like to- know if any recommendations have been made to the minister by the management and officials as to the future development of the plant. Are negotiations in process for the sale of any part of the plant, and when will the committee be able to learn the name of the customer? Are tenders being asked for the sale?
Then, a specific charge has been made that radar was destroyed, and affidavits have been produced in support of that charge. The minister has denied this. Here we have black against white; here are the two poles. There is no in-between. Would the minister say whether radar has been destroyed at the plant of Research Enterprises Limited?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I will answer the questions put by my hon. friend as I remember them. First, he asked, when will the operations of Research Enterprises cease? They will cease in either April or May, 1946. He asked whether negotiations were under way to dispose of the buildings. They are. I cannot give any further answer until the negotiations are closed, without prejudicing the negotiations, but we are carrying on negotiations for a type of operation which will use the same skills that are now used in the plant and which will engage workmen on a scale that we think is exceptionally good for that area. The hon. member asked whether tenders were being called for. They will be called for if we can find a second industry which we think can fill the bill as well, but we consider the maintaining of the same skills in the same area as being more important than getting the last dollar for the sale of the buildings.
Has a. recommendation been received from the management of the plant about this plant?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I think the only recommendation I have seen is the one made by Professor Burton, which has been quoted here. Professor
Demobilization-Reconstruction

Burton was a director of the plant. The management of the plant-I consider the president and the general manager as being the management-have recommended the course of action we are following, namely, that the plant be turned over to a private industry which would engage skills similar to those now being used.
Who recommended that?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The president and the general manager.

I have some recollection of a recommendation being made, possibly by a group of sub-managers or foremen, as to how this plant might be used and maintained as a public enterprise to meet the needs of Canada in radar, optical glass and so on. Am I wrong in that? I think it was last June.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I received a report last June pretty -well along the line that has been mentioned here to-day. The providing of instruments for public schools presents a difficulty from the employment angle because there is not the necessary volume. The question of operating the plant as a non-profit enterprise was carefully considered, but the difficulty was that we could find no line of manufacture which offered a volume sufficient to justify the use of a plant that size.
What about radar?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I have a report on that which I have sent for. There was some equipment which had been spoiled in process and which the management felt they should get rid of. It was destroyed still further, so that the secret process of manufacture would not be revealed. I would prefer to read the report to my hon. friend when I receive it.

I
vould prefer to wait until the minister receives it.

I should like to add a word to what has been said to-day by the hon. member for Eglinton on a subject which I introduced into this house on October 30 last. And I shall not repeat what I said then, because it can be found in Hansard at pages 1658 and 1659. I was very much interested in what the minister said a moment ago in regard to the disposition of Research Enterprises Limited. On Oct. 11 I asked some questions in regard to this industry, which will be found on page 929 of Hansard. The questions were as follows:
Have any suggestions or reports been made to the minister by the administrators of Research Enterprises Limited as to the disposition

of this property or its possible future use? If so, will the minister lay on the table of the house any documents or reports relating thereto?
To which the minister replied1 as follows:
Recommendations have been made. They are made by officers of the department to the minister, and I regard them as confidential documents. It would be impossible to table them at this time, when the disposal of the plant, more or less along the lines of the recommendations, is under consideration. After the transaction is closed and the property has been dealt with I shall be glad to table all the relevant documents.
Would the minister mind tabling that report now? If he cannot d'o so to-day, perhaps at an early date.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I shall be glad' to have another look at the report because I do not even know who prepared it. When I have seen the report I shall give instructions about tabling it.

It would be most instructive to the committee to know just what the director of Research Enterprises thought the future of that plant should be. I do not know just what was recommended, but I would have thought from the observations of Professor Burton and others that they had in mind the retention and operation of the plant, at least for the purposes which were indicated in my speech of October 30 and which have been referred to to-day by the hon. member for Eglinton.
The minister stated a few moments ago that his intention is to retain the buildings which make up the present glass section of the plant as a skeleton to carry out all the operations which were carried out in the Research Enterprises plant itself. I am glad to hear that, because I think that could form the nucleus of a plant which would be of great use to the country in the event of another national emergency, particularly if the personnel who had attained such great skill during the last four or five years were retained1. I only need to repeat what I said before, that it would be a great calamity if this country lost the * benefit of that expert skill which has been developed during these war years. I have no doubt there will be plenty of useful work for them to do at no great expense to the country. I do not think the minister should suggest that we approve expenditures of $8,000,000 a month. I have in mind an expenditure of a few thousand dollars a month.
Reference has been made to the various scientific instruments that could be used by our universities and schools. I should like to refer again to just one thing that was produced at Research Enterprises, viz.: microscopes. Most of us know the optical instrument firm of Zeiss.* That firm was subsidized by the German government and kept in

Demobilization-Reconstruction
operation during the years of peace until it became one of the greatest manufacturers of microscopes -and other precision instruments in the world' and whose products were so valuable during the war. Another reason why the minister should retain that part of the plant is to be found in a recent news report, which I assume is correct, to the effect that Russia had taken over the Zeiss plant in Germany and was moving it to Russia. We should be independent of any foreign country in the production of these scientific instruments so essential for any national emergency. Therefore I urge the minister to retain as much as possible of the facilities of Research Enterprises as well as skilled technicians, which I am glad to learn to-day, he intends to do.
I should like to add a word of commendation for the marvellous work that has been done at that industry during the war years.
I have been through it on a number of occasions. I have admired the efforts made there by the scientists and the workers generally and particularly the work of those in charge of the whole administration, Colonel Phillips, the director, with whom was associated Brigadier Wallace, seconded I believe, from the national research council.
. I spoke on another occasion of the necessity of keeping this plant going in order to provide facilities in arsenal research for the benefit of all the armed services. If this work is to be done in a satisfactory way all the research for the three armed services during the coming years should be centralized under the control of the national research council, which is supported by the government. We know from recent developments that we have not yet reached the limit of armaments for war, that greater and more efficient armaments of destruction will be found, and although that' is a sad prospect, we must continue to do our part in research and in developing improve-' ments to enable us to defend ourselves in the event of another attack. I hope that what has taken place recently in Washington may ultimately result in the control of the atomic bomb and atomic energy. If it does not do so, it is* indeed a sad outlook for the human race.
I shall like to add a word in support of what the hon. member for Eglinton said this afternoon, that research is not sufficiently supported in this country. We have done less than any other country in the world to support research. I hope that the Minister of Reconstruction will remember this and use his influence with the government to have many millions of dollars set aside for purposes of research in Canada. This money, distributed through the national research council 47696-150
would find its way into the laboratories and facilities provided in the universities and medical colleges throughout Canada. We have the facilities in Toronto university as they have in Montreal, Winnipeg and elsewhere for a great expansion in research. All we need is additional money, and I nan think of no department in which money could be spent to greater advantage in the long run than in the promotion of scientific research, Of course, at the moment housing takes priority over everything else.
I wish to say a word in regard to the important part played by the universities of Canada in the problems of reconstruction. The financial burden placed upon the universities in providing educational facilities for our returned veterans must be met by the dominion government, because it is part of their rehabilitation programme and their responsibility.
I might mention briefly how the problem of providing for additional students returning from the war has been met by the university of Toronto. The board of governors were not able to find any buildings in Toronto which could be converted for the use of these returning soldier students, and they were fortunate in being able to arrange with the government, through the Minister of Reconstruction, for the rental of the Ajax buildings built at Pickering, >a distance of some twenty-two miles from Toronto. The cost of alterations and additions to these buildings, plus equipment, to accommodate some 3,000 students will be in the neighbourhood of $786,000, which amount is being provided by the government of Ontario. This property is rented from the dominion government at a cost of $50,000 a year. The courses will begin at Ajax under the aegis of the university of Toronto in January next for some 2,200 returned men.
Next autumn the university of Toronto is planning to provide accommodation for 4,500 students. This will fall short of the number of returned men which it is expected will have to be taken care of. Next year we shall be hard pressed for accommodation, and the university would like to get the Eglinton Hunt club which is now occupied by the air force for research.
If my suggestion of a few weeks ago and again to-day that all scientific research for the three services should be integrated and placed under the national research council were adopted, it should be possible to remove research from Eglinton and give the use of this -building to the university of Toronto. It would be most useful because there are no further buildings available in Toronto. If the university of Toronto is to undertake
