the methods by which we operate. So I say this merely as a suggestion, but having given it some thought and having talked to a number of people'about it. I do not know why legislatures cannot set up some scheme of that kind where a union can voluntarily come, the same as they have voluntarily come for certification. They all said they would not do so; but they have accustomed themselves to that; there is no complaint about it, and they could come and say, "Yes; we want this code; we want a minimum wage; we want union security, and we are doing it on these terms"-because, let hon. members remember this, if by legislation we ever grant union security, then we want to grant the security of the individual against the unions. When a group of men get in charge of a great many men, who perhaps have neither the time nor the inclination to make minute examinations of their problems, we want to know that if some fellow kicks over the traces a little bit he will not lose his security, and his wife will not lose the livelihood of his job when he is put out of that union. We must go that far.
I will now say something about finances, and I do not want somebody to jump on me and) tell me that because the union did not vote for me and I object to their giving a dollar to my opponent, I am not interested in that kind of thing. But I do say this that if we have these people voluntarily coming-and remember it would have to be worked out by experts like the minister, and it could not apply to small shops; you do not need it in craft shops-it would be there for them if they cared to take advantage of it. Again I repeat that we cannot divorce it and put it on the shelf by itself. It must be in conjunction with other conditions, if I may use that expression, "as a part of a general labour code.	.
I am now going to get really bold with the minister and make another suggestion. My criticism-and I may say it is the criticism of my party, because I realize I am speaking for it at the present time-is exemplified to-day in this strike at Windsor. It is that under our legislation, be it provincial or dominion, we have no place to go, after we have had a board of conciliation. We are in the air. We are completely stopped, right there. These boards are usually tliree-men boards, although not necessarily so; why, the minister even called me, and sent me to Nanaimo a few years ago. We brought in a unanimous report-and accomplished exactly nothing. I remember it so very well.
When we are through that, we have no legislation, aside from the boards set up during the war; that is, the regional and dominion war labour boards. But I am really talk-

ing about things in time of peace. I object to a three-man board ever accomplishing anything. Let not the hon. member for Cape Breton South, learned man that he is, think for one moment that I am going to argue compulsory arbitration. I am not. I agreed with him the other night when he said it was the very negation of collective bargaining.
But what I am going to suggest is this, that after the conciliation board is through, and after both reports have been published in the newspapers, there should be another place to go. The reason I say that is this. I base it upon this broad principle, that no lock-out and no strike in the Dominion of Canada can last any appreciable length of time without considerable public support. I make that broad statement without fear of contradiction. Let us be practical.
What happens? We have a board of conciliation, or a regional board, or a war labour board, consisting of three men. We have two men giving a judgment over here, and one over there. They are not boards.. This is the judgment of one man, a man with specially interested counsel pulling on this arm, and another one pulling on that arm. In practice that is really what they are. Certainly the greatest reason for failure we know of is just this, that we publish two judgments -and I intend to call them that.
What happens? We publish two judgments. Two men say this, and the other fellow says that. It is in the newspapers, and I can walk along the street and buy your cheap newspapers and read about it. By the way those newspapers cost only three cents down here; and it took me a number of weeks to find out, because the vendors were not generous enough to tell me. However, I caught on in time.
But what I was going to say was this, that 'the minute we have that situation, what happens? Let us take a cross-section of this House of Commons-and in that connection I am going to refer to a very homely, but not a silly illustration. A week ago last Saturday I attended a football game in this town. The Ottawa Rough Riders were playing against a team from Toronto-
The Argonauts.

Yes, the Toronto Argonauts. I hollered as hard as I could for the Rough Riders. Why? I don't like Ottawa. I didn't know any of the players. But they started nineteen points behind, and I was "for" them in everything they did. They were the under-dogs.
That psychology, Mr. Chairman, carries right through when you read a judgment and find that two men went this way and one

Demobilization-Labour
man that way. The ordinary fellow says, "Those two guys ganged up on him. I am for this guy." That is what happened.
What is the cure? Please do not think I am egotistical, because I am trying to be helpful. My cure is this-I do not wish to be jumped on too quickly, but when I give it I will try to explain and justify it-that there should be a voluntary appeal from any board of conciliation. To whom? I say it should be to a supreme court judge in any province.
I will now answer some of the criticisms. The first one will be this. It used to be said more frequently, but they are not saying it so plainly to-day, because they have learned something about this profession which some of us in the house at least try to honour. It is this, that the only successful lawyer in places where there are many people to-day is the kind of man who quickly learns a new business. You are in a milk investigation today, coal to-morrow, oil the next day, mining the next day, and so on. That is what this business of practising law has become-certainly in the larger centres-in this dominion of Canada. Then again those men are appointed for life. They can only be removed -"on petition", I think is the expression-by an address of both houses of parliament. I may have the wrong word, but the Minister of Justice will know what I mean,
In other words, they have nothing to gain; they have nothing to fear. Remember this, sir, that our civilization is based upon three things, and the judiciary is one of them. It is one of the big props. In good times and in bad times, in war time and in peace time, the judgments of our courts still command the respect; yes, even the admiration, of a very great majority of our people.
Now in these provinces-and I do not mean just one man-let us take four in Ontario, four in Quebec and two in the western provinces. I know that our judges out there are not overworked, although I believe some of them are down here. I am setting out a scheme which is not going to cost this country any money-
And it will probably make you a judge.
Well, I am doing my best, don't you think?
What a hope!

Someone says, "What a hope!" But hope springs eternal. I say seriously that I do not want any new system set up. Let us have no new' commission. In the name of everything that
is reasonable, let us get rid of 150 or so of them, without creating any more. Let us hit upon a ground level-not make a ground loop-so that we shall know where we stand.
What happens then? Well, we will say that I am conducting a law suit with my old friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Perhaps we are very sure that the other is wrong. As a matter of fact I usually think he is wrong, just because I see him sitting over there where he sits to-night. However, that is neither here nor there.
But, supposing we have a lawsuit. What does the ordinary man say? .What do your friends say to you? They say, "Well, Jim MacKinnon had his day in court, and he lost." Perhaps I did not give him a break when I said that; I should have reversed it. But everybody is satisfied that justice has been done-as no doubt it was done.
So I give you this, sir, with respect and great deference, but in my judgment with the assurance that the thing really will work. Let us apply it to the situations that we have today. There is no use in saying that the situation at Windsor is improving if we know that elsewhere in the country it is not improving. The hon. member for Cape Breton South told us about his miners in Nova Scotia, and I know a bit about the miners in another part of the country. I know there is unrest. I know the statement he made the other day, not that it was right, but whether it be right or wrong, that this contest at the Ford plant was regarded by labour-certainly it is regarded so by many who write to me from my own city'-as a threat by that company to break unionism. I am not suggesting that that is true, but I know that is what these men believe. That was the way the thing spread across the country. We cannot just go from one struggle to another. Let us find some broad basis, some reasonable basis. What will happen? I know you cannot make men work by law any more than you can make women sing. There are a lot of things you cannot do by law, but if a person refuses to proceed in a normal and legal manner you can place him in such a position in the public eye that he will lose sympathy, be he employer or be he union.
It seems to me that unless we adopt something of that kind we shall be just jumping from climax to climax, from trouble to trouble, and this great, broad show may come upon us. I hope with all my heart that this trouble at Windsor ends in agreement. I am glad they are trying to agree. I have been in communication with a great many people in this country and I know that if that thing goes wrong we shall not know where our labour
Demobilization-Labour

difficulties will end, and I say that in all seriousness. Until we find that the plan I suggest does not work I hope no one in this committee will say one word which will injure the possibility of its really working.
Now, broadly put, I say that I believe in collective bargaining, and by .collective bargaining I mean bargaining by a strong union. You cannot call if bargaining honestly if the employer has all the money. That just does not make sense. I believe in staying out of the legislative field just as far and as long as we can with respect to things contemplated and things which might be negotiated. We should not feel that we have failed until that conciliation body has had an opportunity of going there and giving one judgment in which the people of this country will believe. Someone may ask me if I believe in an appeal from that judgment. I would say yes, but only one, and that to the Supreme Court of Canada which as a rule delivers only one judgment. I would make it so that there would be only the one judgment at any time.
I close by saying that I know that some people on both sides of the house will not like what I have said. I never knew of legislation that pleased everybody, particularly where you are going to say, "for you, Mr. So-and-so, this is best". I have endeavoured on our behalf to make some contribution, although it may not be complete in detail-I know it is not-to the industrial peace of this country, without which there can be no decent standard of living. We have no greater task; we have no finer ambition and no greater goal could be achieved by the hon. members of this parliament.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure
the committee is grateful to the Minister of Labour for his report of the operations of his department. So far in this appropriation we have been dealing with war departments whose appropriations have been less this year because of the ending of the war. I note that the appropriation for the Department of Labour is somewhat larger than it was last year. I am not complaining about that because I realize that the labour department will be equally as important in the years ahead of us as it has been during the war years.
It would be well if we were to admit at once that the Minister of Labour had a most difficult task during the war. He was dealing with human elements on both sides of production. On the one hand, he was dealing with employers who had the machines and the techniques of 1940 with a social outlook of 1840. On the other hand, he was dealing with

industrial workers who for the first time were being brought together in great numbers in industrial establishments where organization was not only possible but inevitable. He was dealing with a situation where both sides were inexperienced in the work of collective bargaining, and consequently his task was a very difficult one. I agree with the Minister of Labour and with the hon. member who has just taken his seat that if we afe to have progress, peace and prosperity in this country, the cooperation of labour and management and the government as representing the public is an absolute necessity. I will go with the hon. member who has just preceded me and tell the Minister of Labour, or whoever may be sitting in his place at any time while I am here, that he will have my cooperation.
The minister. said that he was opposed to regimentation. I imagine we are all opposed to regimentation; no one likes regimentation, but I am inclined to believe that organized labour and labour generally objected much more to the regimentation of the poverty they had to endure before the war than they did to the regimentation of national selective service which they accepted during the war. I know of a worse state than being frozen in your job; this is, to be frozen out of it. We must avoid, not only the regimentation that may come from official coercion, if you like, but equally the regimentation that comes from the poverty which occurs when 'mass unemployment takes place.
I noticed the minister's reference to P.C. 1003 and the criticism which that order in council has encountered. My attitude toward P.C. 1003 was that it was a step in the right direction but that it did not go far enough. It left out many things that should have been in it and possibly contained some things that were objectionable. But I think the minister is wrong when he says, if I understood him aright, that PjC. 1003 encouraged' the organization of trade unions. I do not think it did. What encouraged the formation of trade unions and what made trade unions inevitable and imperative was the war production that brought workers together and into relations with their employers. That is what addedi to the growth of the trade union movement in this country, and not P.C. 1003. It may have made the situation a little smoother, but whether or not P.C. 1003 was there, trade unionism in this country was bound to grow.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend.
Mr, MacINNIS: Then the minister dealt [DOT]with the wage control order. I think every member of this house agrees that the govern-

Demobilization-Labour
ment made a fair job of controlling prices during the war; we have said that time and time again. But what I have always contended1, and what I think is absolutely true, is that the burden of maintaining prices rested on the shoulders of the low-paid workers. I think that was also the opinion of the national war labour board which, following its inquiry, made recommendations to remedy that condition. I do not think the minister is on very strong ground when he compared conditions in this country with those in France, Belgium and Holland, because the conditions are not at all comparable and he is only making his own case worse by making such a comparison.
Mr. MITCHELL; Just go across to the United States.

That is quite true. I think we made a better job of it than the United States.
Mr. MITCHELL; Or Mexico.

Quite true. But then there is Great Britain, where the situation was much more difficult than here, and Australia, where the situation was equally difficult, and New Zealand. They all made a good job of it because we have learned something all around since the last war.
Mr. MITCHELL; We started the ball rolling.

If the minister insists on taking credit for it, far be it for me to take it away from him.
The minister went on to refer to the international labour office and the resolution which was passed at its 1944 conference, that labour was not a commodity. But surely that must be in contradiction with the government's wage control order which controlled prices and wages ; it controlled wages because labour is a commodity and wages is the price of labour. The commodity nature of labour will not ibe changed by passing resolutions at I.L.O. conferences or anywhere else. Labour will continue to be a commodity so long as it is bought for a price;-wages. We shall not get away from that condition until labour receives its fair share of the nation's wealth because they are entitled to it as human beings. Labour then will come into its own. In saying this, I am not disparaging the work of the international labour office. I think it is doing a great work and I hope that it will continue to do so.
In the time that is left to me I am going to deal with a matter that is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Labour, a matter over which I have felt and still feel great
concern because I consider that we did not deal with it as a democratic nation should have done. I refer to our treatment of persons of Japanese origin who were removed from the Pacific coast early in 1942. I am convinced that our treatment of those people, seventy-five per cent of whom, as the minister pointed out, are Canadians-Canadians, as much as you and I, Mr. Chairman-violated every democratic tradition and every Christian principle. In our dealing with this question there are some things which we should keep constantly before us.
First, our population of Japanese origin is here by our consent. They are in Canada; they came to Canada by virtue of agreements between successive Canadian governments and the Japanese government. That is, those who are Japanese nationals and those who are naturalized Japanese. The seventy-five per cent or more who were bom here are here because we allowed their parents or grandparents to come here. I think it is important to remember that.
The second thing we should remember is that the conditions under which they came into this country and under which they have resided here ever since indicated that we accepted them as permanent residents of this country. The granting of naturalization is an indication of that. Until they were removed from the Pacific coast defence zone in 1942 no question ever arose of returning them to the country of their ancestors. That question1 was never raised.
The minister mentioned the numbers. According to the 1941 census-the total and the categories have changed slightly since- persons of Japanese origin in Canada numbered 23,149, of whom 14,073 were born in Canada, 3,135 were naturalized, 5,890 were Japanese nationals, and persons of Japanese origin, citizens of countries other than Canada or Japan numbered fifty-one. Of the 23,000 here in 1941, 17,200 were Canadian citizens by either birth or naturalization.
The third point which we should keep in mind, but which we very often forget, is that these people were no more responsible for the military aggression of the Japanese government than any other citizen of Canada. Indeed they were not nearly as responsible as the government of this country which insisted on sending war materials to Japan while she was waging war on China.
The fourth point we should keep in mind is that, despite the way we treated them, despite the fact that we uprooted them from their homes; despite the fact that we denied them the rights enjoyed by every other citizen in the country, regardless of racial origin,

Demobilization-Labour
not one disloyal act has been committed by any Canadian-born Japanese, or, as far as I know, by any person of Japanese origin. Let me quote the Prime Minister, who, speaking in this house, on August 4, 1944, said this, as reported in Hansard, at page 5915:
Secondly, account should be taken of the fact that for the most part the people of Japanese race in the country have remained loyal and have refrained from acts of sabotage and of obstruction during the war. It is a fact that no person of Japanese race born in Canada has been charged with any act of sabotage or disloyalty during 'the years of war.
Yet they have been accused of disloyalty and we never gave them an opportunity to demonstrate their loyalty. They wanted to enlist in our armed services; we would not accept them. Why? For fear that when the war was over, they might make claims to citizenship rights which they should have in any event. After repeated requests by the British government for the services of Canadians of Japanese origin to be employed in the Pacific war area a small number of Canadian-born Japanese-some 150 or 160-were allowed to enlist. Some of these are now in India and other parts of the British empire. Some are training in Vancouver, where their fathers and mothers are not allowed to live. Remember, they have enlisted to protect this country. An even worse feature is that after these few were allowed to enlist, a complete censorship was imposed on that fact, and not a word of it came out through press until I brought up the matter here with a question on the order paper.
To demonstrate, that our treatment of this people has come to a point where it makes neither sense nor reason, let me point out that while the finest of our young men were fighting to destroy the concept of building a world order based on race hatred and the master race, we were dealing with this problem solely on the basis of race. Our citizens of Japanese origin were guilty of no crime, and none has been charged against them. Yet, because of the colour of their skin and the accident of their ancestry, they were uprooted from their homes; their property, the accumulation of the labours of a lifetime, was sold without their consent. When they'appealed to our courts of justice-I say, courts of "justice" -justice was refused them. Justice refused to operate; appeals made to the courts in 1943 still remain unanswered. We have heard during the recent weeks a great deal in this house about the rights of citizens and the freedom of the individual. The hon. member

for Lake Centre, speaking here the day before yesterday, said this, as reported in Hansard, at page 2264:
Why was recourse to the courts denied?
That is, to the Eldorado people.
Why was it necessary to deny any individual brought before the commission set up under the order in council the privilege of being represented by counsel? Why was it deemed necessary to deny any person .aggrieved the right of appeal to the courts? Why was it deemed necessary to deny the principle that was enunciated here this afternoon by the Right Hon. Clement Attlee, namely the rule of law, the great principle of this country and of the empire? I protest against this order in council that denies equality under the law, the right of recourse to law, the right to be represented by counsel and, finally, the right in 1945 not to be hailed by subpoena before a star chamber set up by the government for investigation, purposes wherein the individual enters and has no opportunity to defend himself against an investigator who has been invested with powers far and beyond those ever granted to any judge.
Why the necessity for denying any individual rights which have been the rights of freemen since the days of Magna Charta? I think of one paragraph in the Magna Charta which reads as follows:
"To no one will we sell, to no one will we refuse or delay right or justice."
Now, if that applies to this particular company, surely it applies to the 23,000 souls who have done nothing wrong and against whom no charge has been brought.
Would the hon. member permit a question? Is he pleading that the Japanese be allowed to return to British Columbia and to Vancouver?

No; I am not pleading for any such thing, but I am pleading that the Japanese in Canada be treated the same as every other Canadian is treated. That is all I am asking, and that is all they are entitled to. No man is entitled to more and no man should receive less. Let me tell my hon. friend something. The people who are making this problem more difficult than it is, the people who are making it impossible to settle the Japanese across this country, are the people who, because of race hatred and race prejudice, are keeping this situation constantly in a state of unsettlement by refusing to grant the rights of citizenship to the Japanese Canadians. Until we do give them citizenship rights, we shall be faced with the menace of their return to the Pacific coast, once the emergency of the war is over; and the responsibility will rest on those who refuse to make a reasonable settlement possible.
These people are treated as enemy aliens. A case was brought to my attention, a few days before I left home, of a German who

Demobilization-Labour
was a naturalized Canadian. His naturalization was revoked, and 'he told me that he would like to have his Canadian citizenship restored. I took the matter up with the Secretary of State and 'asked him for a report. He very kindly showed me the whole file on this man. Here was a man who was definitely proven to be a nazi agent. But he was free, and so far as I know he could go anywhere he liked in Canada. One man could move wherever he liked, although he was proven to be a nazi agent. Early in August I had a letter from a lawyer in Toronto asking me to try to do something to enable a Canadian of Japanese origin, a man born in British Columbia, to return home to one of the reallocation centres to see his father who was dying. The father sent for his son who was in Toronto. A son and a daughter were living there. This man could not travel without a police permit, although he was a Canadian born in Canada. He had committed no crime and no crime was charged against him; yet he could not go to see his dying father without a permit. He was working; his sister was not; so he gave his permit, to her. When the sister arrived at the home the father insisted on seeing the son. He was his only son, his first-born, and he wanted to see him before he died. I took the matter up with the commissioner in Vancouver, and although it was Saturday afternoon and the office closed, he immediately took steps to get in touch with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and instructed them to issue a permit for this man to travel. He got his permit, but before he reached his father's home his father had died. Can anyone tell me why that man should not be allowed to travel the same as you and I. I will tell you why. The Prime Minister mentioned it in his speech on August 4, 1944. He said this; as reported at page 5917 of Hansard:
We must not permit in Canada the hateful doctrine of racialism which is the basis of the nazi system everywhere.
The reason he could nob travel is that we . have dealt with this problem solely on the basis of race. May I point out here that despite the fine speech made by the Prime Minister on August 4, 1944, nothing has been done up to the present time to solve this problem. The problem cannot be solved until we restore the rights of citizenship to these people. That is a first condition. When he spoke earlier in the evening the Minister of Labour said that there was no coercion used in getting these people to sign the repatriation certificate. I deny that. Only the day before yesterday I was in the office of the Minister of Justice; I saw some of the notices issued); I saw the advertisements. The
advertisements said that refusal to move east might afterwards be taken as disloyalty and be used to ship them to Japan. Remember that when they were asked to move east, they were asked to move east as enemy aliens, without a single right of citizenship, without the right to buy property, without the right to move from one place to another without a police permit.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Six thousand moved
east.
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: They did cooperate.

That is all the more
reason for treating them differently. These people have shown all along that they wanted to cooperate.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Six thousand cooperated and the rest did not.

That is not the way to put it. Under the same conditions I am sure that the Minister of Labour himself would take the same standi as these people took. As a matter of fact, in his speech the Prime Minister said the refusal to accept the conditions which were imposed) upon them should not be taken as disloyalty, because those conditions were- not right. In making his statement last year, the Prime- Minister pointed out that our policy for dealing with this problem should be based on certain- fundamental principles. The first fundamental principle was that steps should be taken so that these people would not return again in large numbers to the Pacific coast. The concern in British Columbia was that this might happen. As I have already said, the danger still remains because of the way in which we have handled this situation.
The minister pointed) out to-night that
9,000	of these people are still in British Columbia, but if we had dealt fairly with them, given them the right to acquire property, to acquire social and economic rights in other parts of -the dominion, these 9,000 people would not now be in British Columbia.
We should deal with them in the way in which, they dealt with the Canadians at Hong Kong. That is the way to treat them.

Speaking in another debate in the house, someone said that we should not have made peace with the Japanese; but that we should have driven the rats into the sea. The Ottawa Journal dealt with that very well in an editorial. The editor said, that
Demobilization-Labour

there were big rats and little rats, and if we were going to drive the little rats into the sea, what was the punishment for the big ones?
Drive them in, too.

But these people in
British Columbia were not at Hong Kong, and neither were the Germans in Canada at Belsen. People who talk like that are talking without an understanding of what British freedom and British justice means.

Nor what Christianity
is.
Nor Christianity.
These people wave the flag all the time too.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Which flag?
Yes, which flag?

The flag you fellows
have taken down. You forget that flag; that is your trouble.
We practise what we preach.

And don't fight
for it.

The second principle
enunciated by the Prime Minister was read by me a little while ago, namely, that no Japanese in Canada had been guilty of any sabotage or disloyal' act. The third fundamental principle was in regard to future immigration into this country. In 1936 I moved a resolution in this house proposing that we do not allow any people into this country to whom we do not extend the full rights of citizenship. That would have applied to the Japanese at that time. But every Liberal member and every Conservative member in the house on that occasion voted against that resolution and. consequently, voted for the continued immigration of Japanese into Canada. That resolution was defeated by 186 to 15. Only the C.C.F. group and some of the Social Credit group voted for it.
It meant votes for the Japanese.
It did not mean votes for the Japanese at all. I will read the resolution for my hon. friend's information. Nothing was mentioned in it about votes for Japanese.

It was a double-barreled,
trick motion.

It was not a double-Darreled trick motion, and when a bill was introduced by the then member for Comox-

Alberni to prohibit Japanese immigration in 1938, I voted for it. But it also was turned down. My resolution was as follows:
Whereas it is detrimental to the best interests of Canada that there should be in the country groups to whom, because of race or religious beliefs, we do not extend all the rights of citizenship;
Therefore be it resolved, that in the opinion of this house, the government should take the necessary measures to exclude from the country all persons belonging to those groups to whom we do not grant the full rights and privileges of citizenship.
That was the resolution, and the reason it was turned down was that we had good trade with Japan at that time when she -was making war on China.
That was not the reason why some of us voted against it.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member cannot make a statement of that kind. He has imputed motives to those who voted down the motion. It was not voted down because of trade but because it was a trick motion that could, be interpreted either way.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think both hon. gentlemen have emphasized their points too strongly. Of course, the words "trick motion" are also out of order.

The wording of the resolution is quite clear. It was well drafted; I drafted it myself. The Prime Minister, when he asked me to withdraw the motion, pointed out that it was a motion for exclusion.
When he spoke in the house on August 4, 1944, he said that he was stating government policy. I doubt very much if it was government policy, even though the Prime Minister stated it. When his followers came to British Columbia they repudiated that policy, although they had not repudiated it on the floor of parliament.
I never changed my views either in this house or out of it. Do not blame me [DOT] for that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member's
time has expired.
Let him go on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: He may continue with the consent of the committee.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Because of your courtesy I shall be brief. I have two or three proposals to make which I believe are absolutely necessary. I think we shall have to deal with this problem on the basis laid down in united nations

Demobilization-Labour
charter which we adopted in this house a few days ago. At the very beginning of that charter we find the following:
We the people of the united nations, determined to safeguard succeeding generations from the scourge of war, which twice in our lifetime has brought untold sorrow to mankind and to reaffirm faith in fundamental human rights, in the dignity and worth of the human person, in the equal rights of men and women and of nations large and small, and to establish conditions under which justice and respect for the obligations arising from treaties and other sources of international law can be maintained
And in the first article we find the following:
To maintain international peace and security, and to- that end: to take effective collective measures for the prevention and removal of threats to the peace, and for the suppression of *acts of aggression or other breaches of the peace, and to bring about by peaceful means, and in conformity of the principles of justice and international law, the adjustment or settlement of international disputes or situations which might lead to a breach of the peace; to achieve international cooperation in solving international problems 'of an economic, social, cultural or humanitarian character; and in promoting and encouraging respect for human rights and for fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race, sex, language or religion . . .
That, in my opinion, is only one way in which we can deal with this problem. Deal with it in accordance with the principles laid down in the united nations charter. I suggest, therefore, to the Minister of Labour and to the government that if they want the Canadian Japanese to settle in the other provinces, the first thing they will have to do is to approach the provinces and get the cancellation of the agreements made with them when these people were moved in. That is essential. It is essential because, if these people's rights as Canadian citizens in other parts of Canada are not guaranteed, we can never settle the problem.
The second thing we should do is to remove the restrictions that now prevent them from buying and leasing real property, so that they can buy property to assure their economic welfare, acquire social and economic roots, and they will have more reasons to remain where they have been settled. These are the things which I believe the government will have to do, and if it begins to do these things immediately, I am sure that this problem will be much more easily solved than we now think possible.

I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Calgary West on the speech which he gave. I enjoyed it very much, and I thought he made a constructive contribution to the debate. In fact, I thought it was one of the most constructive speeches I had heard a gentleman of the legal profession make for some time. He was rather
underestimating the value of the conciliation boards to this country during the very difficult war period. I have had some experience during the last three or four years. I have had an opportunity of serving on three quite important boards, one of which dealt with a serious shipyard situation. From my experience on that board I learned a great deal, and I was amazed, when I came to deal with problems confronting men who came from different backgrounds, with different approaches to life and different outlooks, how much stability had been built into these unions in such a short time. I think those conciliation boards have performed a great service during the war years. I am of this opinion, from my experience, that until we have a national or general labour code, which incorporates labour's rights and labour's responsibilities, we are not going to settle industrial problems, as far as the workers in this country are concerned.
Representing a constituency in which thousands of Japanese have lived since their evacuation from the coastal areas, I wish to say a few words to-night on this important question. It is one which is of serious concern to many of my constituents. I represent a riding which holds a strong affection for the principles of democracy. Their views are not coloured by racial animosity, and they are a people who spring quickly to the defence of democratic principles.
In introducing this subject, I could not give a better background than to read the introduction to the first report made by the security commission to the Department of Labour. This introduction is written in excellent language, and is a good introduction to the subject. I read this from the introduction to the report submitted by the security commission:
The colourful pages of early Canadian history have ever been a recital of action and movement.
The settler, the family, the community; dissension and compromise; a continual readjustment of human lives and their relationships; the urge to seek new and virgin fields, all comprise a tale of natural growth and expansion- and inevitably a westward trek.
Since the linking of east and west by steel, the pattern of our lives has become more uniform and stabilized, our problems more similar -the great war, the boom days and subsequent depression were factors common to the whole country.
Canadian historians could no doubt reveal that, whilst this nationhood is in no small measure the result of the efforts of statesmen and industrial leaders, the ordinary citizen- has also been a contributory factor of considerable importance in the development of Canadian life as it is to-day, and it is significant that the

latter, many of whom still bear the mark of foreign birth or parentage, represent diverse
racial origins.
Canadian people as a whole may have been unmindful of the fact that scattered throughout the dominion were comparatively small groups of people which had not become completely assimiliated into their present environment. This, however, could not be said of the people of British Columbia, who have been constantly kept aware that within the confines of this province, with its wide untenanted areas, lived seven thousand Japanese who had been born in Canada, and sixteen thousand others who had immigrated to this country in the past fifty years.
The lure of this vast continent of plenty had caused most of them to leave their homeland for ever. In general, they were representative of the poorer class in Japan, therefore the most menial work in their new home offered them greater rewards and comforts than those to which they had hitherto been accustomed.^ They proved quick to familiarize themselves with the laws and customs of this country,_ and their apparent slowness to become assimiliated into community life has been, quite probably, due to the existing colour prejudice and the provincial denial of the right to vote. It has been inevitable that the denial of the franchise, and also the restrictions against their entry into certain professions, have of necessity driven them to concentrate their initiative and energy in those- channels of business available to them, and to which they were especially suited. At the outbreak of hostilities, the Japanese in British Columbia were chiefly employed in the fishing industry, boat building, cultivation of truck farms, berries and fruits, and in multifarious types of small businesses such as restaurants, boarding houses, dry-cleaning establishments, and small fruit and grocery stores.
By their industry and self-sacrifice, they had established their homes, families and businesses, seldom becoming public charges, and at all times trusting that some day, they, or at least their Canadian-born children, would have the full privileges of Canadian citizenship.
However, in December of 1941 these hopes were quickly shattered by the unprovoked action of their native countrymen in viciously attacking Pearl Harbor without warning, and this group of people numbering over 23,000 were immediately classified as "alien." Here were represented Japanese who still retained their natural loyalty to the land of their birth. Here also were the indifferent, interested only in their physical and material well-being; and -others, Canadian-born, torn between family ties and an appreciation of this country which they had come to consider their own. There were also others who were entirely uninfluenced by ties of parentage, real Canadians, possessing that spirit of independence which they cherished as their rightful heritage. This group of people of varied objectives, conflicting loyalties and diverse aspirations were now the victims of the cruel action of their race.
I have read that because it is the introduction to the first report of the British Columbia security commission, to the Department of Labour. Following Pearl Harbor, as we. know the government had to take action.

Internments took place, and some were placed in camps. An order for the disposal of Japanese fishing vessels was set up; there was a surrender of moving vehicles, cameras and-weapons, and their property was handed over to the custodian of alien property. A registration of all the Japanese took place, showing at that time 23,312 Japanese resident in British Columbia.
I should like to quote one further paragraph fiom the report where it deals with the creation of the British Columbia security commission. It states:
The government of Canada took no further definite action until public sentiment became inflamed and the members of parliament from this province became so vehement in their denunciation, and the press so vociferous in its expression of indignation that finally, faced with the necessity of establishing some security against possible attack from within as well as without, on March 4, 1942, the government of Canada-
-established the Japanese security commission.
In passing I wish to say this, that the members of that commission were: Austin C. Taylor, chairman; F. J. Mead, assistant commissioner and John Shirras, assistant commissioner. Those gentlemen performed an excellent service to the country and carried out their duties at a very difficult time. A realization that there was a possibility of imminent attack on the coast, and that there was tension throughout British Columbia made the duties of those gentlemen difficult. I give them credit for performing this service in an excellent manner and in most difficult circumstances.
In addition, I wish to associate with those names the names of assistant commissioner Colonel Hill and assistant commissioner Caulkin, both of whom have done excellent work in connection with the Japanese question. When the government was faced with the urgent problem of reallocation of the Japanese in the interior, many people in my constituency offered their cooperation. Officials and residents of municipalities and villages made a definite contribution to the war effort by taking such a democratic and public-spirited approach to the question during those years.
Some minor protests were voiced in my constituency, but they received little general support. Some people who formerly objected to the reallocation of Japanese in my riding are now staunch supporters of the rights of these people as Canadian citizens. There was considerable opposition in British Columbia and there is at the present time. As hon. members know, opposition has been

voiced against the government's policy concerning the Japanese. A few members of parliament representing coastal constituencies have been persistent-and I should think, under the circumstances, somewhat inconsistent-in their opposition to that policy. Some public bodies in British Columbia have taken a similar stand, but even those bodies have had a vacillating policy. I am glad to say that many other public bodies and associations have taken a strong stand for the rights of these people. I find that the more the Canadian people- know about this situation, the more they understand these people and the circumstances; the more inclined to be tolerant they become and the more ready they are to give these people the justice that they deserve.
The policy of the government was outlined by the Prime Minister in his statement last year to the house. The Conservative party has no policy. The attorney general of British Columbia announced that during the last provincial election. Mr. Maitland said that the Conservative party had no policy in connection with the Japanese question. I imagine there are too many decent people who are members or supporters of the Conservative party who do not believe in racial discrimination. That is why the Conservative party has no policy with regard to the disposal of Japanese in British Columbia.
Public bodies have expressed their opinions on this matter, but I want to show how vacillating those opinions have been. I might say that in my own district the farmers' organizations have taken a strong -stand against this racial discrimination against the Japanese. The central farmers' institute of Kootenay West stood firm against racial discrimination. In June, 1943, a meeting of the eastern municipalities of British Columbia held in Kaslo, which I believe is the birthplace of the hon. member for Vancouver South, was opposed, without dissent, to the repatriation of persons of Japanese blood. In August, 1943, at a meeting of the eastern section of the municipalities of British Columbia held in Nelson, a resolution from Richmond, which is a Fraser Valley town, urging repatriation was turned down with no dissenting voice.
In September, 1943, the union of British Columbia municipalities meeting at Port Alberni passed a resolution in favour of repatriation after considerable discussion and with a strong minority vote. In September, 1944, the union of British Columbia municipalities, meeting at Nelson, turned down a similar resolution after debate by a vote of fifty-nine to twenty-eight. In July, 1945, the eastern section of municipalities of British 47696-151
Columbia, meeting at New Denver, turned down a similar resolution with not a single delegate voting for it. In September, 1945, the union of British Columbia municipalities, meeting at Victoria, passed a similar resolution in favour of repatriation with hardly any discussion.
The above shows that there is a strong sentiment against this policy of repatriation, as well as a sentiment in favour. The resolutions passed in favour of repatriation were passed after a great deal of debate and by narrow majorities. So far as my own constituency is concerned, in the winter of 1943, the Nelson citizens' rehabilitation committee, after a number of discussions, finally adopted a brief urging that Japanese-Cana-dians should be encouraged to disperse across Canada and that they should, upon due examination, be given full responsibilities as Canadian citizens and should also bear responsibilities, such as fighting in the armed forces, which they were ready to accept if they had the opportunity. Church and women's organizations and other groups, both in my constituency and throughout British Columbia, are taking a strong stand against this racial discrimination.
I have in my hand a copy of a letter which was circulated by what is known as the white Canada -research committee o-f Fort Langley, British Columbia. This is dated October 2, 1945. I am informed that the sponsors of this committee are the hon. member for New Westminster, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, Mr. A. W. Neill, Mr. J. H. Bose, Major R. A. Payne, Henry L. Edmonds, D. F. Mackay of the native sons of Canada, with Charles E. Hope as honorary secretary. I do not know what is meant by white Canada research committee. After hon. members have heard the contents of this letter, I think they will agree that there is no -research connected with it. This letter was forwarded to all the farmers' institutes in British Columbia in envelopes provided by the superintendent of the farmers' institute. I do not say that he had knowledge of it, but the fact is that the province of British Columbia supplies stationery to the farmers' institutes and this letter was circulated in those envelopes. The letter reads:
Our committee has been urged to get up -a province-wide petition asking the government to repatriate all people of Japanese ancestry now in Canada.
While we are primarily responsible for getting up the enclosed petition, it was thought better to put it out under the name of the Japanese "repatriation committee," as the name "white Canada" brings up the Chinese and

Hindoo questions which might he somewhat controversial, whereas the Japanese question is a problem to itself.
I am enclosing two copies of this petition, also some releases covering different angles of the question. The farmers' institute at its last annual meeting of the advisory board passed some very strong resolutions on the subject- '
That is quite correct; that was at the meeting of the advisory board at Victoria, and1 the farmers' institute of my constituency opposed the resolution.

and we have received a great deal of support from many members, and Doctor Munro, deputy minister of agriculture-
I may say that Doctor Mun-ro is not a doctor of agriculture. He received his doctorate degree as a result of a thesis on the Indians of the Pacific coast. Personally it does not seem right to me that a gentleman who wrote a thesis concerning a native race should assist in the promulgation of this type of doctrine. The letter continues:

and secretary of the advisory board, is also giving us his strong support. Can I ask you to take an active interest in this petition and get signatures in your locality?
Anybody, both men and women, can sign it, whether they are farming or not (storekeepers, railwaymen, et cetera) and if you have a women's institute in your district they also should be asked to get signatures, as this is a matter of the most vital importance to everybody in this province, and indeed to all Canada.
There have been some similar petitions circulated, but there is no reason why all these petitions should not be signed by the same people but I should caution you that no one should sign more than one copy of the same petition, and no one under the age of fourteen should be asked to sign; above that age I think they should, as in two or three years this Japanese question will be vital to them also.
I might just say in passing that these are the very same people who raised such a strong objection to anyone being allowed to vote at the age of eighteen years. The letter continues:
If you are not able to handle this yourself, could you get two or three of your neighbours to handle it, taking a day or two each. Time is important and we should have all the petitions ready for presntation to parliament within the next month or two.
I also enclose a subscription list which was got out at the suggestion of the native sons' organization at New Westminster, and successfully circulated there. If anyone in your locality cares to subscribe anything, bis contribution will be welcomed, no matter how small. Perhaps your institute would like to help. The total cost will be about $800, no salaries of any kind are being paid, but printing, stamps and stenography cost money. I want, however, to strongly emphasize that the signatures to the petition are the important thing, subscriptions to the cost are quite secondary.

Mr. Austin Harris of Steveston is kindly helping to circulate these petitions and correspondence in connection with them should be directed to him; he will also send you further copies of the petition on request.
Hoping for your wholehearted cooperation, I am,
Yours faithfully,
Charles E. Hope, honorary secretary,
per Austin Harris.
I realize fully the difficulties the government has encountered1 in connection with this question. Considering the time of war and the outlook of the people in general, I believe that on the whole the government policy has been reasonably fair and reasonably decent. It is only fair to say that, because this whole movement of people no doubt has been carried out under great difficulties. I know something about it, because I had something to do with the commissioners. Thousands of these people lived in my district; I moved among them a great deal and tried to get to know them and to know the facts. Undoubtedly injustices have been done. Mistakes have been made by officials, and no doubt that was inevitable in time of war and stress, but every effort should be made to rectify them.
I wish to make a few criticisms of government policy. The government made a great mistake in not enlisting Japanese men of military age. If we had followed the policy pursued in the United States, a satisfactory solution of this problem would be much less difficult in the days to come. After the statement of the Prime Minister, Canadian-born citizens of Japanese racial origin were enlisted in the Canadian army. The public are largely unaware of the fact that hundreds of them enlisted and that every one was a general service man.
With regard to the sale of assets, , the Japanese property at the coast was handed over to the custodian of enemy property on the definite understanding that it would be held in trust for them. Instead, it has been sold without the permission of the owners, and very often at ridiculous prices. The Japanese war veterans who received a grant of lands after the last war have now had it taken from them. Goods of real value were sold without the owner's knowledge, while, in some cases, articles of only sentimental value have been returned to their owners. Things for which there was no market have in many eases been destroyed. Test cases were brought before the exchequer court to determine the legality of the government's action in selling their property. The court sat in June, 1944; but as yet, November, 1945, no decision has been handed down -by Mr. Justice Thorson.

In the meantime, although the matter is before the courts, the sale of property has been pressed. Very few of these people still retain very much of what they possessed at the coast, and' the proceeds of the sales have been used to support the owners so that now very few have anything left at all. From inquiries I have made-and I am not one to make rash statements in a matter of this kind-I believe that a grave injustice has been done to thousands of Japanese people. Their property is being sold at ridiculous prices on what the labour department reports is a seller's market.

I should now like to say a word on the repatriation policy. In April a detachment of the Royal Canadian Mounted1 Police with selective service placement officers came to all the larger Japanese settlements in British Columbia offering them this alternative: You may choose to go to Japan after the war with your way paid and all your assets, or you may choose to remain in Canada; but, if you choose Canada, you must move east of the Rockies, or it will be a black mark against you when the loyalty commission comes around. This commission to determine the loyalty to Canada of persons of Japanese origin was promised by the Prime Minister in August, 1944, but as yet is not in existence.
In the proclamation announcing the choice before all people of Japanese origin, citizens and aliens alike, it was made to appear that to choose Japan would be far more profitable than to choose Canada. A very large majority chose "return to Japan". But when their reasons and intentions are looked into it does not appear that many really desire to go there. Although Japanese nationals were given to understand that if they chose Canada they would have to go east immediately, now when they try to go they find it is almost impossible to get a permit. Some nationals, it is true, have been able to get a permit and go, but they are definitely exceptions. The fact that these men and women are nationals rather than Canadian citizens in a great many cases does not reflect upon them. In many cases it is due to one of three reasons: (1) the vagaries of our naturalization laws; (2) lawyers who were charged with putting through their clients' applications for naturalization failed to do so; (3) naturalizations which have taken place since 1922 are not accepted as valid. The result of all this has been to create a great ferment in the minds not only of the 47696-151i
people of Japanese origin but of many occidentals in Canada as well. Business men, women's institutes, women's auxiliaries and women's missionary societies up and down the valley as well as missionaries of the United and Anglican churches, have wired or written the Prime Minister, the Minister of Labour, and leading church authorities. At present an appeal direct to the throne is being considered. So far the results seem to be nil.
Without a doubt the present situation is, in my opinion, absolutely opposed to the principles which Canada is professing to support, in the united nations as outlined in the preamble to the charter. It is also opposed to the words of the Prime Minister of this country in 1944, when he stated that racial discrimination will not be allowed to gain a foothold in this country. The root of the whole trouble appears to be in the delay of the government in admitting the rights and duties of Canadian citizens. If the government would make up its mind as to what Canadian citizenship means, the whole situation would be rapidly simplified. People of Japanese origin in this country know that in the panic days of Pearl Harbor it was inevitable that some injustices should take place. They are very fair in that respect. I know, because I have spoken to hundreds of them, but if they are given a square deal any sense of injury and personal injustice will, I am sure, rapidly fade away.
